parties:
Bangladesh ------ Appellant
vs. 
Yakub Sardar & ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J:-The question involved in this appeal by special leave is of considerable public importance. It is whether the Sessions Judge has got power under S. 439A, Criminal Procedure Code or under any other provision of the Code to direct a Magistrate to send the case to him for trial when the Magistrate dismissed the complaint under section 203 of the Code. 

 2. The matter has arisen from C.R. Case No. 420 of 1980 of the Court of Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Shariatpur, along with G.R. Case No. 106 of 1980, corresponding to Sessions Case No. 51 of 1981. The case has run a zigzag course for a period of over 9 years. For the purpose of deciding the question raised before us the relevant facts thereof may be briefly stated below. 

 3. One Mansur Sarder of village Chardhupuria, P.S. Janjirawas murdered on 5 April 1980 and on the following day Yakub Sarder, a relation of the deceased, lodged a First Information Report (FIR) whereupon the police investigated the case and submitted charge-sheet against a number of persons and thereupon the G.R. Case No. 106 of 1980 was started. This case was sent by the Magistrate to the Court of Session, Faridpur (subsequently, Shariatpur) for trial and was registered as Sessions Case No. 51 of 1981. This case, it appears, is still pending for trial before the Sessions Judge. 

 4. But 10 days after the murder of Mansur Sarder, his son Abdul Hye Sarder filed a Complaint-petition before the same Magistrate alleging that the facts stated in the first information report lodged by Yakub Sarder were not correct and that having returned home 10 days after the death of his father he collected true facts of the case from his mother and sister and then filed the complaint against a number of persons including Yakub Sarder alleging that they were the real culprits. This complaint was registered as C.R. Case No. 420 of 1980, as already referred to. The Magistrate after examining the complainant on oath sent the case to the Officer-in-Charge of the Police-Station, Janjira for enquiry and report. A Criminal Motion (Criminal Motion No. 78 of 1980) was moved before the Sessions Judge against the order for enquiry, and the learned Sessions Judge directed the Magistrate to follow the provisions of section 205-D of the Code. The complainant thereafter filed an application to withdraw from the proceeding and ultimately the Magistrate by an order dated 10 April 1981 dismissed the complaint for default. Amir Khan, a nephew of the deceased, who was cited as a witness in the complaint and as an accused in the F.I.R., filed Criminal Motion No. 118 of 1981 against the order of dismissal of the complaint whereupon the learned Sessions Judge by an order dated 24 June 1981 directed the Magistrate for, what appears to be, further enquiry under section 436 Cr. P.C. Thereupon, the Magistrate examined 7 witnesses and on consideration of the evidence dismissed the complaint under section 203 Cr. P.C. by an order dated 4 November 1982. This order of dismissal was again challenged in revision (Criminal Motion No. 518 of 1982) before the Sessions Judge who by an order dated 17 January 1983 set aside the Magistrate's order and directed the Magistrate to send the record of the CR. Case to him treating the same to be a counter-case of the Sessions Case No. 51 of 1981 which is already pending before him. This order of the Sessions Judge was challenged before the High Court Division in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 14 of 1983 and in this case a Division Bench, by an order dated 17 August 1983, set aside the Sessions Judge's order and quashed the proceeding of the C.R. Case observing that when the Magistrate dismissed the complaint the Sessions Judge, as a court of original jurisdiction, had no power to directly entertain such a case for trial "unless the accused has been sent" to him by the Magistrate. 

 5. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General, has referred to the relevant orders recorded in the Order-Sheet of this case and has pointed out that the learned Judges of the High Court Division proceeded on a wrong assumption that no cognizance was taken by the Magistrate in the complaint case but the Sessions Judge has taken cognizance in disregard to the mandatory prohibition of section 193 Cr. P.C. Section 193 provides that except as otherwise expressly provided no Court of Session shall take cognizance of any offence as a court of original jurisdiction unless the accused has been sent to it by a competent Magistrate. In this case, cognizance is found to have been taken by the Magistrate himself on 14 April 1980 when he examined the complainant on solemn affirmation under section 200 Cr.P.c. The Magistrate, however, without issuing any process against the accused under section 204, thought it proper to have the matter enquired under section 202 Cr. P.C. After the Magistrate has issued process against the accused and the offence involved is exclusively triable by a Court of Session, the Magistrate shall send the case to the Court of Session under section 20S-C. In this case cognizance was taken by the Magistrate who however did not issue any process but dismissed the complaint. The exact question before us is when the Magistrate did not issue any process against the accused but dismissed the complaint against them, whether the Sessions Judge has got power to direct the Magistrate to send the case to him so that he can try the case as a Court of Session. 

 6. The Sessions Judge and, for that purpose, the District Magistrate, Chief Metropolitan Magistrate and the High Court Division, got power under section 435 Cr. P.c. to call for the record of any case pending before any Magistrate and direct the Magistrate under section 436 to make further enquiry into any complaint which has been dismissed under section 203 or sub-section (3) of section 204 Cr. P.C. In this case when the complaint was dismissed by the Magistrate the Sessions Judge had got power to direct further enquiry into the matter. But by the impugned order dated 17 January 1983 the learned Sessions Judge did not direct further enquiry but asked the Magistrate to . send the case to him so that he could try it along with the G. R. Case already pending before him knowing full-well that the accused were not yet summoned by the Magistrate, that is, no process was yet issued against them. The learned Additional Attorney General has tried to argue that the impugnederder of the Sessions Judge was in fact made in his revisional power under S. 439A Cr. P.C. This section was inserted in the Code by a recent amendment conferring upon the Sessions Judge all the powers in revision which are exercisable by the High Court Division under S. 439 Cr. P.C. The learned Additional Attorney General has also referred to the now-repealed s. 437 Cr. P.C. under which the Sessions Judge had power to make an order for commitment of the accused for trial by a Court of Session if the accused had been improperly discharged by the Magistrate It may be mentioned here that S. 437 related to the committal proceeding under Chapter XVIII Cr. P.C. containing Sections 206 to 220. When that Chapter, that is, the provision for commitment of any accused by a Magistrate, was in force and when in a case exclusively triable by a Court of Session the accused was discharged under section 209, the Sessions Judge got the power to make order for direct commitment of the accused to him. Now that the committal proceeding had been deleted, section 437 lost its reason of existence and as such it was rightly repealed. The learned Additional Attorney General has, however, tried to seek some guidance from the repealed provision of the law and argued that in the instant case involving an offence under sections 302/34 Penal Code, which is exclusively triable by a Court of Session, and when the Magistrate spite of sufficient materials revealed during the preliminary enquiry under s. 202 Cr.P.C., dismissed the complaint on two occasions, the Sessions Judge got implied power under S. 439A Cr.P.C. to call for the records of the case from the Magistrate so as to try it himself. We find it difficult to accept this view and to hold that the revisional power, whether of the Sessions Judge or of the High Court Division, includes by implication the power to try an accused against whom no process has been issued under section 204. Under the repealed section 437 Cr. P.C., it may be kept in mind, an order for commitment could be made after the accused was brought before court by issuing process and then was discharged under section 209. It is true that under S. 439A, the Sessions Judge has got all the powers which the High Court Division has under S. 439 Cr. P.C. This power includes the power of a court of appeal under sections 423, 426, 427, 428 Cr. P.C.; the power to order for trial of an accused against whom no process has been issued is not included therein. The learned Additional Attorney-General has argued that when the Sessions Judge has got power to call for the record of a case disposed of, or pending before, a Magistrate and when the Sessions Judge upon examination of the record of the case finds that there are sufficient materials for putting the accused to trial the next inevitable step will be to ask the Magistrate to forward the case to him for holding the trial the offence involved being exclusively triable by him. The learned Additional Attorney-General has referred to the impugned order of the Magistrate dated 4 November 1982 by which he dismissed the complaint The order is quoted below: 

 "Heard both the parties today and examined the case records. Since the police has submitted C.S. in another case of the same occurrence and cognizance has been taken, I think there is no scope to continue this complaint case any more. Moreover no prima facie case has been made out during enquiry. The case is, therefore, dismissed u/s. 203 Cr. P.C." 

 7. The main ground cited by the Magistrate for dismissing the complaint is that the Police have submitted charge-sheet in the other case arising from the same occurrence. The Magistrate is palpably wrong in taking the view that when the police has submitted charge-sheet in the case started on a First Information Report the Magistrate has no power to issue process against the accused cited in the complaint petition. The Magistrate while considering the complaint arising from a case about which the police have submitted charge-sheet must confine himself to the evidence produced before him and if on such evidence a prima facie case is made out he will issue process. Thereafter the trial Court will see whether both the cases will be tried according to the established practices and procedure for trial of cross-cases. That the police have submitted charge-sheet cannot be a ground for dismissing the complaint as has been done by the learned Magistrate. The learned Magistrate has of course stated that "moreover, no prima facie case has been made out during the enquiry". This is obviously a secondary ground the main ground for dismissal of the complaint is that the police submitted charge-sheet in the other case. The Magistrate should have considered whether any process should have been issued in view of the evidence of the witnesses examined keeping in mind that he is not holding trial at this stage. When the complaint was dismissed in this case on an erroneous view of law, the only course for the Sessions Judge was to direct further enquiry under section 436  Cr. P.C. This section has remained unaffected by the recent amendment and this power is independent of the power under S. 439A. The revisional power of the Sessions Judge under S. 439A, as we find clearly, does not include the power to try a case in which no process has yet been issued by the Magistrate. Such power is also not available to the High Court Division either under section 439 Cr. P.C. 

 8. The learned Additional Attorney-General has, however, submitted that if in a case where the Magistrate, inspite of sufficient evidence against the accused, has refused to issue process, the High Court Division may interfere in its inherent power under section 561-A Cr. P.C. and order for summoning the accused for trial in the appropriate court. This is purely a hypothetical question for in the instant case the High Court Division did not exercise such power. On the contrary, learned Judges of the High Court Division quashed the proceeding. This order of the High Court Division is not sustainable in law. The proper course for the High Court Division was to modify the Sessions Judge's order and to direct further enquiry under section 436. 

 9. Mr. Afzalur Rahman, learned Advocate for the accused respondents while conceding that the High Court Division's order quashing the proceeding is not supportable, has argued that in view of the long pendency of the case and the relationships between the parties who have been taking conflicting stands, an order for further enquiry will not be justified. Having taken into consideration all aspects of the matter, we think that, in the interest of justice, further enquiry should be made into the complaint which we find to have been improperly dismissed. 

 10. In the result, the appeal is allowed and the impugned order of the High Court Division is set aside and it is directed that further enquiry be made into the complaint of CR. Case No. 420 of 1980.
